cards.q: A rectangular garden is 50 m long and 30 m wide. What is its area?
cards.why: Area of a rectangle = length × width = 50 × 30 = 1500 m². (2 × 50 + 2 × 30 = 160 is the perimeter, not the area.)
cards.hook: Area: multiply the sides. Perimeter: add all the way round.

cards.q: A square has sides of length 2k cm. Which expression gives its area, in cm²?
cards.why: Area = side × side = 2k × 2k. Multiply the numbers (2 × 2 = 4) and the letters (k × k = k²), so the area is 4k².
cards.hook: Square the whole side: (2k)² = 4k². The 2 gets squared too.

cards.q: A triangle has a base of 12 m and a perpendicular height of 1.5 m. What is its area?
cards.why: Area of a triangle = ½ × base × height = ½ × 12 × 1.5 = 9 m².
cards.hook: A triangle is half a rectangle: ½ × base × height.

cards.q: A cube has sides of length 4 cm. What is its volume?
cards.why: Volume of a cube = length × width × height = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 cm³.
cards.hook: Volume multiplies three lengths: cm × cm × cm = cm³.

cards.q: A circle fits exactly inside a square of side 10 cm, touching all four sides. What is the radius of the circle?
cards.why: The circle touches opposite sides, so its diameter is the side, 10 cm. The radius is half of that: 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm.
cards.hook: Circle in a square: diameter = side. Then halve it.

cards.q: A wheel has a diameter of 12 cm. What is its circumference, in terms of π?
cards.why: Circumference = 2πr. The radius is 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm, so 2 × π × 6 = 12π cm (the same as π × diameter).
cards.hook: Circumference = 2πr = πd. The formula with r² is the area.

cards.q: A circle has a radius of 5 cm. What is its area, correct to one decimal place?
cards.why: Area = πr² = π × 5² = 25π = 78.539… ≈ 78.5 cm². Square only the radius, not π.
cards.hook: Area = πr²: square the radius first, then multiply by π.

cards.q: A cylinder has radius 5 cm and height 3 cm. What is its volume, in terms of π?
cards.why: Volume of a cylinder = πr²h = π × 5² × 3 = π × 25 × 3 = 75π cm³.
cards.hook: Cylinder volume: area of the circle × height, πr²h.

cards.q: A closed can has radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. What is the area of its curved side, in terms of π?
cards.why: Unrolled, the side is a rectangle: circumference 2πr by height h. 2πrh = 2 × π × 3 × 10 = 60π cm² (no ends).
cards.hook: Unroll a can's label: one side is the circumference, the other the height.

cards.q: A ball has a radius of 10 cm. What is its volume, correct to the nearest cm³?
cards.hook: Sphere volume: (4/3)πr³. Volume is cubic, so cube the radius.

cards.q: A ball has a radius of 5 cm. What is its surface area, in terms of π?
cards.why: Surface area of a sphere = 4πr² = 4 × π × 5² = 4 × 25π = 100π cm².
cards.hook: A sphere's skin is four circles of its own radius: 4πr².

cards.q: A hemisphere has a radius of 6 m. What is its volume, in terms of π?
cards.why: A hemisphere is half a sphere: V = (2/3)πr³ = (2/3) × π × 6³ = (2/3) × 216π = 144π m³.
cards.hook: Half of (4/3) is (2/3): a hemisphere holds (2/3)πr³.

cards.q: A cone has radius 3 cm, vertical height 4 cm and slant height 5 cm. What is its volume, in terms of π?
cards.why: V = (1/3)πr²h, using the vertical height: (1/3) × π × 3² × 4 = (1/3) × 36π = 12π cm³.
cards.hook: A cone is a third of the cylinder around it: (1/3)πr²h.

cards.q: A cone has radius 3 cm, vertical height 4 cm and slant height 5 cm. What is its curved surface area, in terms of π?
cards.why: Curved surface area of a cone = πrl, where l is the slant height: π × 3 × 5 = 15π cm².
cards.hook: Cone's curved surface: πrl, and l is the slant, never the height.

cards.q: A cone has base radius 3 cm, height 4 cm and slant height 5 cm. Its curved surface is cut open into a sector. What is the radius of the sector?
cards.why: The sector's straight edges run from the tip of the cone down to the rim of the base: they are the slant height, 5 cm.
cards.hook: Unroll a cone: its slant height becomes the sector's radius.

cards.q: A cone has base radius 3 cm and slant height 5 cm. Its curved surface opens out into a sector. How long is the sector's arc, in terms of π?
cards.why: Rolled up, the arc goes once round the base, so it is the base's circumference: 2πr = 2 × π × 3 = 6π cm.
cards.hook: A cone's net wraps round the base: arc = circumference of the base.

cards.q: When you use the trapezoidal rule to estimate an area, which of the heights get multiplied by 2?
cards.right: All except the first and last
cards.why: Area ≈ (h/2)[(first + last) + 2(all the rest)]. An end height is the edge of one strip; each middle height is shared by two strips.
cards.hook: Ends once, middles twice: each middle height serves two strips.

cards.q: A lake is measured from a straight line across it. At one point its edge is 12 m above the line and 8 m below it. What width goes into the trapezoidal rule there?
cards.why: The width is the whole way across the lake: the part above the line plus the part below, 12 + 8 = 20 m.
cards.hook: Measured on both sides of a line? Add the two for the full width.

cards.q: Which change is most likely to make a trapezoidal rule estimate of an area more accurate?
wrong: Double the first and last heights
Leave out the first and last heights
cards.why: The rule swaps each curved strip for a straight-sided trapezium. Narrower strips follow the curve more closely, so the error is smaller.
cards.hook: More, thinner strips hug the curve better.
keys: Narrower strips follow the curve more closely

cards.q: How many cm³ are there in 2 litres?
cards.why: 1 litre = 1000 cm³ (a cube 10 cm × 10 cm × 10 cm), so 2 litres = 2 × 1000 = 2000 cm³.
cards.hook: A litre is a 10 cm cube: 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 cm³.

cards.q: One litre of paint covers 4 m². How many litres of paint are needed to cover 50 m²?
cards.why: Each litre covers 4 m², so find how many 4s go into 50: 50 ÷ 4 = 12.5 litres.
cards.hook: Area ÷ area per litre = litres.

cards.q: Each cm³ of gold weighs 19.3 g. A gold bead has a volume of 2 cm³. How many grams of gold is it?
cards.why: Every cm³ weighs 19.3 g, so 2 cm³ weighs 2 × 19.3 = 38.6 g.
cards.hook: Grams per cm³ × cm³ = grams.

cards.q: A cone has radius 6 cm and vertical height 8 cm. What is its slant height?
cards.why: Radius, height and slant make a right-angled triangle: l² = 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100, so l = √100 = 10 cm.
cards.hook: The slant is the hypotenuse: l² = r² + h², then square root.

cards.q: A square has sides of 8 cm. A circle, centred at the middle of the square, passes through all four corners. What is its radius, to 2 decimal places?
cards.why: Centre to corner is 4 across and 4 up (half the side each way): r² = 4² + 4² = 32, so r = √32 = 5.656… ≈ 5.66 cm.
cards.hook: Through the corners: the radius is half the diagonal. Use Pythagoras.

cards.q: A sector has a radius of 10 cm and an angle of 90° at the centre. What is the length of its arc, in terms of π?
cards.hook: A sector is a slice: (angle ÷ 360) of the whole circle.

cards.q: A cone has base radius 3 cm, height 4 cm and slant height 5 cm. Its net is a sector of radius 5 cm. What is the angle at the centre of the sector?
cards.why: The arc is the base's circumference: (θ/360) × 2π(5) = 2π(3). The 2π cancels, so θ = 360 × 3 ÷ 5 = 216°.
cards.hook: Cone's net angle = 360 × base radius ÷ slant height.

cards.q: Use the trapezoidal rule: the strips are 2 m wide and the heights are 3, 5, 6 and 4 m, in order. What is the estimated area?
cards.hook: Half the width × (the two ends + twice all the middles).

cards.q: The strips are 4 m wide and the heights are 3, x and 5 m, in order. The trapezoidal rule gives an area of 40 m². What is x?
cards.hook: Fill in the rule with x, set it equal to the area, then solve.

cards.q: On a scale diagram, 1 cm stands for 3 m. Each grid box is 0.5 cm tall. A line is 6 boxes tall. What is its real length?
cards.why: 6 boxes × 0.5 cm = 3 cm on the diagram. Each cm is 3 m, so 3 × 3 = 9 m in real life.
cards.hook: Boxes → cm → metres: change one step at a time.

cards.q: A cone holds 600 cm³. Water flows in at 0.5 litres per minute. How long does it take to fill the cone, in seconds?
cards.why: 0.5 litres = 500 cm³ a minute. 600 ÷ 500 = 1.2 minutes, and 1.2 × 60 = 72 seconds.
cards.hook: Same units first (cm³ with cm³), then minutes × 60 = seconds.

cards.q: A cylinder, partly full of water, has radius 5 cm. A stone of volume 50π cm³ sinks to the bottom, fully under water. By how much does the water level rise?
cards.why: The rise is a cylinder of radius 5 holding the stone's volume: π × 5² × h = 50π, so 25πh = 50π and h = 2 cm.
cards.hook: Volume put in = πR² × rise.

cards.q: A cylinder has a volume of 100π cm³ and a radius of 5 cm. What is its height?
cards.why: πr²h = 100π, so π × 25 × h = 100π. Divide both sides by 25π: h = 4 cm.
cards.hook: Put in what you know, then divide by everything stuck to h.

cards.q: A tank is a cylinder of radius 3 m and length 10 m with a hemisphere of radius 3 m on each end. What is its volume, in terms of π?
cards.why: Cylinder: π × 3² × 10 = 90π. Two hemispheres make one sphere: (4/3)π × 3³ = 36π. Total: 90π + 36π = 126π m³.
cards.hook: Two hemispheres = one whole sphere.

cards.q: A hollow rubber ball has an outer radius of 5 cm and an inner radius of 2 cm. What volume of rubber is in it, in terms of π?
cards.why: Rubber = outer sphere − inner sphere = (4/3)π(5³ − 2³) = (4/3)π(125 − 8) = (4/3)π × 117 = 156π cm³.
cards.hook: Hollow? Whole volume minus the hole. Cube each radius on its own.

cards.q: A shed is a prism 10 m long. Its front is a rectangle 6 m wide and 3 m tall with a triangle on top (base 6 m, height 2 m). What is its volume?
cards.why: Front face = 6 × 3 + ½ × 6 × 2 = 18 + 6 = 24 m². Volume of a prism = face area × length = 24 × 10 = 240 m³.
cards.hook: Prism: area of the end face × length.

cards.q: A closed box is 2 cm long, 3 cm wide and 4 cm tall. What is its total surface area?
cards.why: Three pairs of rectangles: 2(2 × 3) + 2(2 × 4) + 2(3 × 4) = 12 + 16 + 24 = 52 cm².
cards.hook: A box has 6 faces in 3 matching pairs: find 3, then double.

cards.q: A crescent is left when a disc of radius 2 cm is cut out of a disc of radius 3 cm. What is the area of the crescent, in terms of π?
cards.why: Area left = big disc − small disc = π × 3² − π × 2² = 9π − 4π = 5π cm².
cards.hook: Area by subtraction: the whole area minus the part cut out.

cards.q: A crescent is left when a disc of radius 2 cm is cut out of a disc of radius 3 cm (the circles touch at one point). What is the crescent's perimeter, in terms of π?
cards.why: Trace round it: the whole outer circle and the whole inner circle are its edges. 2π × 3 + 2π × 2 = 6π + 4π = 10π cm.
cards.hook: Perimeter: trace every edge and add them, inner edges too.

cards.q: A square has side 5 cm. A tilted square inside it has its corners on the sides, cutting off 4 right-angled triangles with sides 3 cm and 2 cm. What is the area of the tilted square?
cards.why: Big square: 5 × 5 = 25. Each corner triangle: ½ × 3 × 2 = 3. Tilted square = 25 − 4 × 3 = 13 cm².
cards.hook: Awkward shape? Take the easy pieces away from the whole.

cards.q: A circle of area 50 cm² is drawn inside a square of area 64 cm². What percentage of the square does the circle cover, to the nearest percent?
cards.hook: Percentage of the whole: part ÷ whole × 100.

cards.q: You need 22 litres of paint. It is sold in 5 litre tins at €20 a tin. How much does the paint cost?
cards.why: 22 ÷ 5 = 4.4 tins. You can't buy part of a tin and 4 is not enough, so buy 5 tins: 5 × €20 = €100.
cards.hook: Tins, buses, boxes: always round up to whole ones.

cards.q: A garden is 20 m by 10 m and has a pond of area 30 m². Sowing grass costs €2 per m². What does it cost to sow grass on all of it except the pond?
cards.why: Grass = garden − pond = 20 × 10 − 30 = 170 m². Cost = 170 × €2 = €340.
cards.hook: Find the area really being covered first, then × the price.

cards.q: Two touching wheels turn without slipping. Wheel A has radius 3 cm and wheel B has radius 6 cm. B makes 10 full turns. How many turns does A make?
cards.why: Both rims move the same distance: 10 × 2π(6) = 120π cm. One turn of A is 2π(3) = 6π, so 120π ÷ 6π = 20 turns.
cards.hook: Touching wheels roll the same distance: the smaller one turns more.

cards.q: Three balls of radius 3 cm fit exactly in a closed cylinder, one on top of another. What is the volume of the cylinder, in terms of π?
cards.why: The radius is 3 and the height is three diameters: 3 × 6 = 18 cm. V = πr²h = π × 9 × 18 = 162π cm³.
cards.hook: Stacked balls: height = number of balls × diameter.
